title: Did Caesar Really Say "Et tu, Brute?" A Plot of Over 60: Who Heard It?
description:
"Et tu, Brute?" may be the most borrowed last words in the world. This episode follows the line from March 15, in Pompey's meeting hall, all the way back to the stage. Suetonius, in The Deified Julius, first writes that through 23 blows Caesar said no complete sentence, only groaning at the first blow; he then keeps a Greek version that some have handed down, και συ τέκνον ("You too, child?"), and Brutus's name is not in the quoted words. Plutarch's Life of Caesar and Life of Brutus do not bear witness to the Latin line, and since they are by the same author, they do not count as two independent witnesses. In Act 3 of Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Caesar first says the Latin "Et tu, Brute?", then the English "Then fall, Caesar!", and only then comes the stage direction "Dies". Later, a footnote in an English translation of The Twelve Caesars guessed that Caesar would probably have said the line in Latin; that is the editor's conjecture, not ancient text. We can be sure how the play is written; whether Caesar said the Latin line, the records cannot say for certain, and they cannot show the reverse either, that he never said anything like it.

Suetonius follows the Rolfe Latin text and English translation at PerseusDL; Plutarch follows the Clough English translation at GITenberg (not checked against the Greek original); Shakespeare follows the full text at GITenberg. Sources are listed below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated; the historical figures are cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant as likenesses, not images of the actual scene.

Information as of 2026-10-20 (rewritten under new rules on 2026-10-25)

thumbnail.headline:
Et tu?
**Who Heard It?**
thumbnail.sub: In the biography: three Greek words

et101.text: You've probably heard someone betrayed by a friend quote Caesar: "Et tu, Brute?"

et102.text: These are probably the world's most borrowed last words; behind them lies a plot of over 60 people.

et103.text: On a wooden stage, the actor playing Caesar has just sat down; another leans in.

et104.text: Brutus's actor raises a prop dagger; the scene freezes before Caesar speaks.

et105.text: But in history, there were two Brutuses that day: one urged Caesar out the door. Where would the other stand?

et106.text: This file opens three biographies by two ancient authors, to see where this line really comes from.

et107.text: Did the real Caesar actually say this line before he died?

et201.text: That stage dagger began, in history, with a list of plotters.

et202.text: The biographer Suetonius recorded the ringleaders; Cassius was one of them.

et203.text: The two Brutuses from the opening were both among them: Marcus and Decimus.

et204.text: Same name, same side; on my first read, I too had to stop and sort them out.

et206.text: They weighed several spots to strike, and finally chose a Senate meeting.

et207.text: On March 15, senators would gather in Pompey's meeting hall.

et208.text: This hall stood beside Pompey's theater; Plutarch also recorded where it was.

et209.text: I'd guess their logic was simple: on a meeting day, Caesar must show up, right?

et210.text: Meanwhile, under Caesar's statue, words appeared mocking him as kinglike.

et211.text: On Marcus's own tribunal, too, someone left anonymous notes urging him to act.

et212.text: Plutarch says the other plotters wanted Marcus's prestige to give the deed more weight.

et213.text: Think of him as the banner the whole plan flew.

et214.text: Decimus also joined the plot, yet Caesar still trusted him. How much?

et215.text: Suetonius writes of Caesar's will: Decimus was named among the heirs in the second degree.

et216.text: The same will even made several of Caesar's killers guardians of any son he might have later.

et217.text: So which of the two Brutuses would personally lead Caesar out of his house?

et301.text: Getting him out did take persuading: that morning, Caesar considered staying home.

et302.text: Suetonius notes he felt unwell, and the omens from the sacrifice were bad.

et303.text: Plutarch writes that his wife Calpurnia urged him to put off the meeting.

et304.text: You've had that kind of morning: unwell, and someone at home says stay in today.

et305.text: Dreams and omens: biography tales. Did they stop Caesar in the end?

et306.text: They didn't. Then one Brutus came to urge him: the senators are waiting, don't let the meeting fall through.

et307.text: Caesar took his advice and left home.

et308.text: The Brutus who coaxed him out was Decimus, the one in the will.

et309.text: This part gives me chills every time.

et310.text: On the way, someone handed Caesar a plot warning.

et312.text: He tucked it among the other papers in his hand, to read later.

et313.text: You've likely done this: an important letter stacked with junk flyers, to look at later.

et314.text: Plutarch also records the warning, but says the crowd pressed in and Caesar couldn't finish it.

et315.text: The warning was in his hand, yet didn't stop him. Who waited in the hall?

et401.text: The plotters themselves, who were already at Pompey's portico.

et402.text: Caesar was late, and the waiting made them ever tenser.

et403.text: You've waited on a latecomer; waiting for this, every minute would probably drag.

et404.text: Then a senator quietly told Marcus and Cassius he hoped they'd finish it quickly.

et405.text: They briefly thought it had leaked.

et406.text: Then the man turned to talk to Caesar. Would he betray them?

et407.text: Marcus watched the man's face and judged he was only petitioning Caesar.

et409.text: Another plotter kept Antony talking outside the door.

et410.text: Caesar went in and sat; a petitioner came right up. What would Caesar say first?

et501.text: The first to speak was the petitioner: Tillius Cimber, pleading for his exiled brother.

et502.text: Caesar refused, and Cimber seized his toga.

et503.text: Suetonius records that Caesar first cried out: "This is violence!"

et504.text: Notice: this cry came before the first blow; it isn't the famous dying question.

et505.text: Next, a man named Casca struck; was Caesar still in time to fight back?

et506.text: He was. He seized the man's arm, and Suetonius says he even struck back with his stylus.

et507.text: Honestly, that stylus made me do a double take.

et508.text: Plutarch, Life of Caesar: after the first blow, Caesar challenged Casca in Latin.

et509.text: Casca then called to his brother for help; Plutarch says in Greek.

et510.text: So that Greek was Casca's. And Caesar himself: did he speak Greek later?

et511.text: Nearby senators froze in terror, neither fleeing nor helping.

et512.text: If you were there, I'd guess you'd freeze too.

et513.text: Caesar tried to move outward, but drawn daggers were all around.

et514.text: The other Brutus from the opening question is right here.

et515.text: Plutarch's Life of Brutus says Marcus, dagger in hand, stepped in front of Caesar.

et516.text: So Caesar let go of Casca's arm and pulled his toga over his head.

et517.text: Facing him was Marcus. Did any ancient author record Caesar's last words?

et601.text: Suetonius first writes: through 23 blows, Caesar didn't utter one complete sentence.

et602.text: He records only that Caesar groaned once, at the first blow.

et603.text: If you think the story ends here, so did I at first.

et604.text: But this Latin passage doesn't end at the groan.

et605.text: The author goes on: yet some have handed down different words.

et606.text: He doesn't name them, or say he was there to hear it.

et607.text: In that account, as Marcus rushed in, Caesar spoke to him, and in Greek.

et608.text: Three Greek words, roughly: "You too, child?"

et609.text: Brutus's name isn't in the quote; it's in the sentence introducing the rumor.

et610.text: Nor does "child" prove the two were related by blood.

et611.text: Calling someone younger "child" doesn't make them your own.

et612.text: Would the other author, Plutarch, add evidence for those three Greek words?

et613.text: Plutarch's Life of Caesar relays one account: Caesar fell at the foot of Pompey's statue.

et614.text: That passage gives him no last words to Marcus either.

et615.text: In the Life of Brutus: once Caesar fell, Marcus tried to explain, but senators fled; no one listened.

et616.text: And both are by the same author, so they aren't two independent eyewitnesses.

et617.text: This, I think, is easiest to miss.

et618.text: Of course, unrecorded doesn't prove it never happened.

et619.text: Then who plainly wrote this Latin line into a play?

et701.text: It's that frozen stage from the opening. Now the actor playing Caesar goes on.

et702.text: Shakespeare has petitioners crowd in; Caesar claims he's as constant as the northern star.

et703.text: Seen enough plays, you know: when a character talks this big, trouble is coming.

et704.text: Casca cries, "Speak, hands, for me!" The stage direction has him and the others stab.

et705.text: The script even spells out that Marcus Brutus stabs too.

et706.text: What would Caesar say to him?

et707.text: The famous line finally comes, but only the half "Et tu, Brute?" is in Latin.

et708.text: The rest, "Then fall, Caesar!", is English in this version.

et709.text: That is the play's last line for Caesar; only then comes a one-line stage direction: Dies.

et710.text: On first reading, I went back and reread that line.

et711.text: As he falls, the play's plotters shout for liberty.

et712.text: Remember Plutarch's Marcus, who tried to explain but no one listened?

et713.text: On stage, Brutus calms the crowd: Caesar's ambition was punished.

et714.text: So what the play proves is that Shakespeare wrote the line, not that Caesar said it.

et715.text: Nor does the play prove Shakespeare was the first to write it.

et716.text: You might think: surely this Latin line has some ancient source?

et717.text: Later, an English translation of The Twelve Caesars put a Latin guess in a footnote; which layer will readers misread?

et801.text: That translation's text, though, still keeps "some authors relate."

et802.text: Only it renders the address as "my son," not "Brutus" as in Shakespeare.

et803.text: That sentence carries note 97; turn to the footnote and you see another language.

et804.text: You've likely skipped many footnotes too; this time, the key is hidden right there.

et805.text: Only there does a later editor guess Caesar likely said it in Latin.

et806.text: There's no verbatim record there; "the probability is" marks it as the editor's conjecture.

et807.text: The editor also judged that long address too wordy for an emergency.

et808.text: His reasoning: at such a moment, why would Caesar switch to Greek?

et809.text: Honestly, I've had that doubt too; but a doubt isn't evidence.

et810.text: Does the footnote give the ancient source you wondered about?

et811.text: The footnote only notes Greek variants in manuscripts; it cites no ancient copy with the Latin line.

et812.text: So that's the layer readers misread: an editor's reasoning, not Suetonius's words.

et813.text: Back to our opening question: did Caesar really say that line before dying?

et814.text: What he actually said before dying, this file can only mark: unresolved.

et815.text: Next time you hear a famous historical quote, ask: is it in the ancient text, a translation's footnote, or on stage?

et816.text: First heard this line in a textbook, a film, or a play? Tell me in comments.

et817.text: This channel sticks to the record; subscribe to open the files together.
